question: On 14 November 2025, the Munich-based auction house Hermann Historica planned to sell personal effects of victims of German Nazi concentration camps. Among the items up for auction were a prosthetic leg from the Dachau camp and a comb and spoon belonging to prisoners of the Auschwitz-Birkenau camp, engraved with the names and camp numbers of their owners.

The auction was ultimately cancelled after a wave of outrage and protests from Polish and Jewish communities, as well as reactions from the President of the Republic of Poland and the Israeli Government.

In light of the above: Does the Commission intend to propose binding EU legislation obliging auction houses and galleries operating within the Union to immediately report information about the sale of items from the Second World War, in particular personal belongings of victims and material evidence of crimes committed by German Nazis, to the relevant state authorities and memorial institutions (such as the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum)?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.2.2026) The Commission unequivocally condemns the crimes committed by the Nazis and their collaborators, and any actions that deny, distort or trivialise the Holocaust. The Commission remains firmly committed to ensure the Holocaust remembrance.

As stated in its Strategy on combating antisemitism and fostering Jewish life (2021-2030)1, the Commission will cooperate with industry and IT companies to prevent the illegal display and sale of Nazirelated symbols, memorabilia and literature online. The Commission has not identified EU level legislation governing the specific situation described by the Honourable Member.
The Commission will continue to monitor developments and assess if additional measures may be needed.
